newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan corporate sentiment turns down; stocks fall.
newsitem.headline: Japan corporate sentiment turns down; stocks fall.

text.p: Japan's central bank Wednesday reported an unexpected drop in a key survey of corporate sentiment, which sent stocks lower and the dollar soaring as economists predicted the data would slam the door on any hike in Japanese interest rates.
Tokyo stocks ended near their lows for the day, with the Nikkei 225 stock average down 200.46 points or 0.96 percent at 20,709.81.
The dollar climbed as high as 108.47 Japanese yen in Far East trading, and the U.S. currency opened at 108.25 yen in New York, up from 107.70 at Tuesday's close.

The Bank of Japan's quarterly corporate survey, or "tankan," showed the diffusion index for major manufacturers -- an important gauge of business sentiment -- falling to minus seven in August from minus three in the previous survey in May.
Analysts said the weak corporate sentiment survey sharply curtailed the chances of an interest rate rise this year.
Japan's central bank sought to put the best face on the data, which defied economists' predictions of improving sentiment and was the first drop in business sentiment in a year.

"Although the recovery is not without setbacks, the doors to the recovery have not been shut," Masayuki Matsushima, director of the central bank's Research and Statistics Department, told a news conference.
Most economists surveyed by Reuters had expected the major manufacturers' index to rise.
Much of the drop in the due to deteriorating conditions in basic materials industries such as steel, chemicals and petroleum.
The index represents the percentage of firms expecting business to improve minus those who expect it to worsen. The higher the number, the more optimistic the outlook.
Economists said the latest figures would make it impossible for the Bank of Japan to tighten its current easy money policy, probably for the rest of the year.

The central bank slashed its official discount rate, at which it lends to commercial banks, to 0.5 percent last September to prevent the economy from sliding into recession. It has been held short-term market rates low as well.
"All the speculation (about rate rises) will fade to the sidelines, and that will allow them to stay on course," said Kenneth Courtis, chief economist at Deutsche Capital Markets.

Financial markets as recently as last month had speculated that the central bank was poised to tighten rates. But worries that the economic recovery would lose steam later in the year had already dampened those expectations.
Analysts said prospects that Japanese interest rates would stay low while U.S. rates might rise could well drive the yen down further.
